[Dolmabahçe Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolmabah%C3%A7e_Palace "Dolmabahçe Palace") is a popular tourism destination in Turkey.

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Istanbul_asv2020-02_img60_Ortak%C3%B6y_Mosque.jpg/250px-Istanbul_asv2020-02_img60_Ortak%C3%B6y_Mosque.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Istanbul_asv2020-02_img60_Ortak%C3%B6y_Mosque.jpg)

[Ortaköy Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ortak%C3%B6y_Mosque "Ortaköy Mosque") and the [Bosphorus Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosphorus_Bridge "Bosphorus Bridge")

[Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul") is one of the most important tourist spots not only in [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") but also in the world. There are thousands of hotels and other tourist-oriented industries in the city. Turkey's [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Turkey "List of cities in Turkey"), Istanbul has a number of major attractions derived from its historical status as the capital of the [Byzantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") and [Ottoman Empires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"). These include the [Sultan Ahmed Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_Ahmed_Mosque "Sultan Ahmed Mosque") (the "Blue Mosque"), the [Hagia Sophia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia "Hagia Sophia"), the [Topkapı Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topkap%C4%B1_Palace "Topkapı Palace"), the [Basilica Cistern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_Cistern "Basilica Cistern"), the [Dolmabahçe Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolmabah%C3%A7e_Palace "Dolmabahçe Palace"), the [Galata Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galata_Tower "Galata Tower"), the [Grand Bazaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Bazaar,_Istanbul "Grand Bazaar, Istanbul"), the [Spice Bazaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spice_Bazaar,_Istanbul "Spice Bazaar, Istanbul"), and the [Pera Palace Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pera_Palace_Hotel "Pera Palace Hotel"). Istanbul has also recently become one of the biggest shopping centers of the European region by hosting malls and shopping centers, such as [MetroCity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetroCity_AVM "MetroCity AVM"), [Akmerkez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akmerkez "Akmerkez") and [Cevahir Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cevahir_Mall "Cevahir Mall"), which is the biggest mall in Europe and seventh largest shopping center in the world. Other attractions include sporting events, museums, and cultural events.

In January 2013, the Turkish government announced that it would build the world's largest airport in [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul"). The operation has an invested 7-billion euros and was planned to have the first part of a four-part plan completed by 2017.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-investvine-12)

### Ankara

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_Turkey&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Ankara")]

Ankara is the country's capital and second most populated city.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-13) It is rich with Turkish history and culture that have roots in the founding of Turkey along with the history of ancient civilizations. The most popular landmark is the [Anıtkabir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An%C4%B1tkabir "Anıtkabir"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-14) a mausoleum for [Atatürk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atat%C3%BCrk "Atatürk"), the founder of the Republic of Turkey. Another landmark would be the [Museum of Anatolian Civilizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Anatolian_Civilizations "Museum of Anatolian Civilizations"), a museum that possesses works from [Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleolithic "Paleolithic"), [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic"), [Hatti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hittite_empire "Hittite empire"), [Hittite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hittites "Hittites"), [Phrygian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phrygia "Phrygia"), [Urartian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urartu "Urartu"), and [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") civilizations.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-15)

### Izmir

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_Turkey&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Izmir")]

[Izmir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%B0zmir "İzmir") is a city with historical and geopolitical importance in ancient civilizations such as [Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_(ancient_kingdom) "Macedonia (ancient kingdom)"), [Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), [Lydia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydia "Lydia"), and the [Ottomans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-16) The city has a memorable history in the early years of Turkey as it was the main city that was affected by the [Greco-Turkish War (1919–1922)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Turkish_War_(1919%E2%80%931922) "Greco-Turkish War (1919–1922)").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-17) Izmir is home to many ancient cities such as [Ephesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephesus "Ephesus"), [Pergamon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pergamon "Pergamon"), and [Klazomenai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klazomenai "Klazomenai").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-18) Besides historical significance, Izmir also possesses many locations for coastal tourism for international travelers. Frequently visited regions that have tourist beaches for local and international tourists would be [Çeşme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%87e%C5%9Fme "Çeşme"), [Mordoğan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordo%C4%9Fan "Mordoğan"), and [Foça](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fo%C3%A7a "Foça").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-20)

[Butterfly Valley, Fethiye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butterfly_Valley,_Fethiye "Butterfly Valley, Fethiye")

Beach vacations and [Blue Cruises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Cruise "Blue Cruise"), particularly for Turkish delights and visitors from [Western Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe "Western Europe"), are also central to the Turkish [tourism industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_industry "Tourism industry"). Most beach resorts are located along the southwestern and southern coast, called the [Turkish Riviera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Riviera "Turkish Riviera"), especially along the Mediterranean coast near [Antalya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antalya "Antalya"). Antalya is also accepted as the tourism capital of Turkey.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-21) Major resort towns include [Bodrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodrum "Bodrum"), [Fethiye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fethiye "Fethiye"), [Marmaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marmaris "Marmaris"), [Kuşadası](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku%C5%9Fadas%C4%B1 "Kuşadası"), [Didim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didim "Didim") and [Alanya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alanya "Alanya"). Also, Turkey has been chosen second in the world in 2015 with its 436 blue-flagged beaches, according to the Chamber of Shipping.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-22)

Attractions elsewhere in the country include the sites of [Ephesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephesus "Ephesus"), [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy "Troy"), [Pergamon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pergamon "Pergamon"), [House of the Virgin Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_the_Virgin_Mary "House of the Virgin Mary"), [Pamukkale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamukkale "Pamukkale"), [Hierapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierapolis "Hierapolis"), [Trabzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabzon "Trabzon") (where one of the oldest monasteries is the [Sümela Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%BCmela_Monastery "Sümela Monastery")), [Konya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konya "Konya") (where the poet [Rumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumi "Rumi") had spent most of his life), [Didyma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didyma "Didyma"), [Church of Antioch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Antioch "Church of Antioch"), ancient Pontic capital and king rock tombs with its acropolis in [Amasya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amasya "Amasya"), religious places in [Mardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mardin "Mardin") (such as [Deyrülzafarân Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deyr%C3%BClzafar%C3%A2n_Monastery "Deyrülzafarân Monastery")), and the ruined cities and landscapes of [Cappadocia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia "Cappadocia").

One of the most important and famous cities in the east and [southeast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Anatolia_Region "Southeastern Anatolia Region") of Turkey is called [Diyarbakır](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diyarbak%C4%B1r "Diyarbakır"). This city is considered one of the important options for traveling to the east of Turkey due to its numerous historical, religious and cultural places. For researchers who are interested in [cultural studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_studies "Cultural studies"), this city is a favorable option for study and research due to the accommodation of different ethnic groups ([Kurds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurds_in_Turkey "Kurds in Turkey"), Turks, [Arabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs_in_Turkey "Arabs in Turkey"), [Assyrians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assyrians_in_Turkey "Assyrians in Turkey"), [Armenians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenians_in_Turkey "Armenians in Turkey")) and religious groups ([Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Turkey "Islam in Turkey"), [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_Turkey "Christianity in Turkey")). Due to the civil wars between the [PKK group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurdistan_Workers'_Party "Kurdistan Workers' Party") and the [central government of Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Turkey "Government of Turkey") in the 90's, the number of tourists in this region decreased. With the beginning of the 21st century and after the establishment of relative peace and security in these areas, tourism has been increasing again in these areas.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-28)

[Cumalıkızık](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumal%C4%B1k%C4%B1z%C4%B1k "Cumalıkızık") is an old town from [early Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_architecture "Ottoman architecture") era in [Bursa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bursa "Bursa")

[Gallipoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallipoli "Gallipoli") and Anzac Cove – a small [cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cove "Cove") on the [Gallipoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallipoli "Gallipoli") peninsula, which became known as the site of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") landing of the ANZAC ([Australian and New Zealand Army Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_and_New_Zealand_Army_Corps "Australian and New Zealand Army Corps")) on 25 April 1915. Following the [landing at Anzac Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_at_Anzac_Cove "Landing at Anzac Cove"), the beach became the main base for the Australian and New Zealand troops for the eight months of the [Gallipoli campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallipoli_campaign "Gallipoli campaign").

[Cappadocia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia "Cappadocia") is a region created by the erosion of soft volcanic stone by the wind and rain for centuries.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-Capadocia-29) In the picture is the classic hot air ballon showing.The area is a popular tourist destination, having many sites with unique geological, historic, and cultural features.

[Safranbolu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safranbolu "Safranbolu") was added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage sites in 1994 due to its well-preserved Ottoman era houses and architecture.

As of 2023, Turkey hosts 21 [UNESCO World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Turkey "List of World Heritage Sites in Turkey"), 19 cultural and 2 mixed.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-30)

## Medical tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_Turkey&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Medical tourism")]

Main article: [Health care in Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_care_in_Turkey "Health care in Turkey")

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Ac%C4%B1bademHospitalAltunizade_%281%29.jpg/250px-Ac%C4%B1bademHospitalAltunizade_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ac%C4%B1bademHospitalAltunizade_(1).jpg)

Acıbadem Hospital in Altunizade, [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul")

An emerging branch of tourism in Turkey is [medical tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_tourism "Medical tourism"). Commonly performed medical procedures are [hair transplant operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hair_transplantation "Hair transplantation"), [rhinoplasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhinoplasty "Rhinoplasty"), [cosmetic dentistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmetic_dentistry "Cosmetic dentistry"), [bariatric surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bariatric_surgery "Bariatric surgery"), [buttock augmentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buttock_augmentation "Buttock augmentation"), [mammaplasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammaplasty "Mammaplasty") and [mastopexy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastopexy "Mastopexy") as it draws in thousands of foreigner tourists every year.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-32) In 2021, the revenue generated from medical tourism was given as $1.05 billion with 642,000 people that visited for the purpose of getting medical service.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-33) This is due to Turkey offering high-quality clinics for affordable pricing compared to the rest of Europe and its central location between Asia and Europe.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-34) Other reasons for the high demand for healthcare in Turkey are foreigners having easy visa procedures and immediate scheduling for operations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-richtmann.org-1)

Turkey issued 16,199,968 electronic visas between April 2013 and 1 January 2017. The acceptance rate was 87.79% as 18,452,733 applications were filed in this period. ### Explain

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_Turkey&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Explain")]

Foreign tourist arrivals increased substantially in Turkey between 2000 and 2005, from 8 million to 25 million, which made Turkey a top-10 destination in the world for foreign visitors. 2005 revenues were US$20.3 billion which also made Turkey one of the top-10 biggest revenue owners in the world. In 2011, Turkey ranked as the 6th most popular tourist destination in the world and 4th in Europe, according to [UNWTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Tourism_Organization "World Tourism Organization") World Tourism barometer.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-WTO2012Highlights-40) See [World Tourism rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Tourism_rankings "World Tourism rankings"). At its height in 2014, Turkey attracted around 42 million foreign tourists, still ranking as the 6th most popular tourist destination in the world.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-42_million_tourists_visit_Turkey_in_2014_-_Daily_Sabah-41) From 2015, tourism to Turkey entered a steep decline.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-csmonitor-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-43) In 2016, only around 30 million people visited Turkey. 2016 is described as the second year of huge losses on both visitor numbers and income, a "year of devastating losses", with Turkish tourism businesses stating that they "cannot remember a worse time in the sector".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-three-5) The number of foreign visitors started recovering in 2017 with 37.9 million visitors being recorded. The recovery was partly due to intense security campaigns and advertising. The number of Russian tourists increased by 444% after the recovery of bilateral relations, resulting in Russia becoming the top tourism market for Turkey once again.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-hur2017fig-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-itij-8) Increases were also recorded in the British, Dutch and Belgian markets.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-44)

In early 2017, the Turkish government urged Turkish citizens living abroad to take their vacations in Turkey, attempting to revive the struggling tourism sector[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-45) of an economy that went into contraction from late 2016.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-46) After the April 2017 [constitutional referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_constitutional_referendum,_2017 "Turkish constitutional referendum, 2017"), another sharp drop in tourist bookings from Germany was recorded.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-47) In 2018, however, the German Tourism Industry Association recorded a growth in German tourist bookings for Turkey, with a 70% increase being recorded by the [TUI Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TUI_Group "TUI Group") alone.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-48)

## Government policy and regulation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_Turkey&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Government policy and regulation")]

Tourism policy and official promotion in Turkey are handled largely through the [Ministry of Culture and Tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Culture_and_Tourism_(Turkey) "Ministry of Culture and Tourism (Turkey)") and related public bodies. Travel agencies operate under Law No. 1618 on Travel Agencies and the Association of Travel Agencies, which regulates agency establishment, licensing, services, inspection and consumer-related obligations.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-49) A travel agency operating licence is issued by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, while agencies become members of the Association of Turkish Travel Agencies (TÜRSAB).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-50)

The Türkiye Tourism Promotion and Development Agency (TGA), established in 2019 as a related entity of the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, carries out national tourism promotion, destination development and communication activities in line with government tourism policy.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-51) Turkey has also introduced an Environmental and Cultural Sustainability Program for the tourism industry. Its criteria apply to accommodation facilities and tour operators, and are aligned with Global Sustainable Tourism Council standards.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-52)

The [AKP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_and_Development_Party_(Turkey) "Justice and Development Party (Turkey)") government has been promoting "[halal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halal "Halal") tourism" for years,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-bbc-53) politically reaffirming this stance over the course of 2016.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-54) In March 2017, a Turkish court banned global travel fare aggregator website [Booking.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booking.com "Booking.com") from offering services to Turkish tourists for lack of a national licence,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-55) while the Hoteliers Association of Turkey campaigns for the lifting of the ban on the enterprise on which its members relied for up to 90 percent of their turnover.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-56) In April 2017, the police department of the prime resort city of [Antalya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antalya "Antalya") issued a directive banning the consumption of alcohol outside of buildings.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-57)

## COVID-19 pandemic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_Turkey&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: COVID-19 pandemic")]

During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Turkey "COVID-19 pandemic in Turkey"), the number of tourists arriving in [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") declined to around 16 million in 2020.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-:02-58) This was the lowest number of tourists in the last decade.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-:02-58) The revenue from international travel was reduced to $13.7 billion which only made up 1.91% of the total economy in 2020.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-60) In 2021, Turkey's tourism recovered from the pandemic as it contributed $59.3 billion to the GDP, which made up 7.3% of the total economy.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-62)

## Travel advisories by foreign governments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_Turkey&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Travel advisories by foreign governments")]

A number of foreign governments warn travelers about risks related to [human rights in Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Turkey "Human rights in Turkey"). The United States, Germany, Austria, Sweden, the Netherlands, and Belgium warn of [arbitrary detention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitrary_arrest_and_detention "Arbitrary arrest and detention"), arrest, prosecution, or exit bans, while France, the United Kingdom, Denmark, Switzerland, Finland, Norway, and Australia also caution that political statements or [social-media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media "Social media") activity (including "likes") can result in criminal penalties.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-69) Germany specifically warns that participation in [Kurdish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurdish_population "Kurdish population")-related demonstrations, petitions, or legally registered associations in Germany can lead to arrest, exit bans, or refusal of entry in Turkey.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-70)

The [Government of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Canada "Government of Canada") similarly warns that Turkish authorities have detained or prosecuted people for critical political expression, including social-media posts made outside Turkey or years earlier, and advises travelers to "Avoid discussions (including on social media) on historical and religious issues as well as on politics."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-71) On 23 November 2024, Canadian journalist [Neil Hauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Hauer?action=edit&redlink=1 "Neil Hauer (page does not exist)") was refused entry to Turkey, told he was on a blacklist and detained for about 16 hours; Turkish authorities did not publicly disclose why he had been blacklisted.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-72) Hauer suggested that the ban may have resulted either from his critical reporting on Azerbaijan and [Nagorno-Karabakh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagorno-Karabakh_conflict "Nagorno-Karabakh conflict") or from his posts about the [Armenian genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide "Armenian genocide").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Turkey#cite_note-73)

# Turkey - statistics & facts

 Region  Türkiye  Türkiye 

 Choose a region: ![Image 2: Türkiye](https://cdn.statcdn.com/static/icons/flag/iso/svg_flags/TR.svg) Türkiye 

*   [Overview](https://www.statista.com/topics/1442/turkey/#topicOverview)
*   [Editor’s Picks](https://www.statista.com/topics/1442/turkey/#editorsPicks)
*   [Statistics](https://www.statista.com/topics/1442/turkey/#statisticChapter)

 After a period of constant increase, [Turkey’s population](https://www.statista.com/statistics/263753/total-population-in-turkey/) surpassed the 80-million mark in 2017, with10 million inhabitants more than a decade earlier. At the same time, the [fertility rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/255459/fertility-rate-in-turkey/) in the country is decreasing: in 2016, it was down to 2.05 children per woman, a decline from 2.24 children per woman only ten years prior. 

  
 Turkey is one of the most important industrial and emerging countries (G20), and one of the so-called “Next Eleven” – the most important emerging countries after the four [BRIC states](https://www.statista.com/topics/1393/bric-countries/) Brazil, Russia, India and China. It is ranked 17th among the [countries with the largest gross domestic product (GDP)](https://www.statista.com/statistics/268173/ranking-of-the-20-countries-with-the-largest-gdp/) with [its own GDP](https://www.statista.com/statistics/263757/gross-domestic-product-gdp-in-turkey/) amounting to approximately 852 billion U.S. dollars in 2017. In 2017, [economic growth in Turkey](https://www.statista.com/statistics/263612/growth-of-the-gdp-in-turkey/) declined to about 7.44 percent after dropping near 3 percent the prior year. The current outlook for economic growth is modest.   
  
 Turkey’s [GDP per capita](https://www.statista.com/statistics/263599/per-capita-gross-domestic-product-gdp-in-turkey/) was at approximately 10,537 U.S. dollars in 2017 and is drop in the medium term, recovering by 2022. The [unemployment rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/263708/unemployment-rate-in-turkey/) dipped to 8.1 percent in 2012. However, it has increased again and is estimated to stay above 10 percent for the next few years. [Turkey’s inflation rate](https://www.statista.com/statistics/277044/inflation-rate-in-turkey/) has increased recently and is expected to be high for the foreseeable future.   
  
 In 2017, Turkey[exported goods](https://www.statista.com/statistics/255647/export-of-goods-from-turkey/) worth about 157 billion U.S. dollars and [imported goods](https://www.statista.com/statistics/255659/import-of-goods-from-turkey/) worth approximately 233.8 billion U.S. dollars. Thus, it is not one of the [main export countries](https://www.statista.com/statistics/264623/ranking-of-the-leading-export-countries-worldwide/) nor one of the [main import countries](https://www.statista.com/statistics/268184/largest-importing-countries-worldwide/) worldwide in that year.   
  
 Turkey’s main trade partners are Germany, the UK, and the United Arab Emirates for [export](https://www.statista.com/statistics/255650/main-export-partners-of-turkey/) and China, Germany, and Russia for [imports](https://www.statista.com/statistics/255665/main-import-partners-of-turkey/). Its [national debt](https://www.statista.com/statistics/277040/turkish-national-debt-in-relation-to-gdp/) is rather low at an estimated 28 percent of GDP as of 2017, while the [fiscal deficit](https://www.statista.com/statistics/255677/budgetary-balance-of-turkey-in-relation-to-the-gross-domestic-product/) amounted to approximately 2.3 percent of GDP the same year.

Turkey,[a] officially the Republic of Türkiye,[b] is a country mainly located in Anatolia in West Asia, with a smaller part called East Thrace in Southeast Europe. It borders the Black Sea to the north; Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Iran to the east; Iraq, Syria, and the Mediterranean Sea to the south; and the Aegean Sea, Greece, and Bulgaria to the west. Turkey is home to over 86 million people;[7] most are ethnic Turks, while Kurds are the largest ethnic minority.[4] Officially a secular state, Turkey has a Muslim-majority population. Ankara is Turkey's capital and second-largest city. Istanbul is its largest city and economic center. Other major cities include İzmir, Bursa, and Antalya.

First inhabited by modern humans during the Late Paleolithic,[11] present-day Turkey was home to various ancient peoples.[12] The Hattians were assimilated by the Hittites and other Anatolian peoples.[13] Classical Anatolia transitioned into cultural Hellenization after Alexander the Great's conquests, and later Romanization during the Roman and Byzantine eras.[14] The Seljuk Turks began migrating into Anatolia in the 11th century, starting the Turkification process.[15] The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum ruled Anatolia until the Mongol invasion in 1243, when it disintegrated into Turkish principalities.[16] Beginning in 1299, the Ottomans united the principalities and expanded. Mehmed II conquered Constantinople (modern-day Istanbul) in 1453. During the reigns of Selim I and Suleiman the Magnificent, the Ottoman Empire became a global power.[17] From 1789 onwards, the empire saw major changes, reforms, centralization, and rising nationalism while its territory declined.[18]

In the 19th and early 20th centuries, persecution of Muslims during the Ottoman contraction and in the Russian Empire resulted in large-scale loss of life and mass migration into modern-day Turkey from the Balkans, Caucasus, and Crimea.[19] Under the control of the Three Pashas, the Ottoman Empire entered World War I in 1914, during which the Ottoman government committed genocides against its Armenian, Greek, and Assyrian subjects.[20][21][22] Following Ottoman defeat, the Turkish War of Independence resulted in the abolition of the sultanate and the signing of the Treaty of Lausanne. Turkey emerged as a more homogenous nation state.[23] The Republic was proclaimed on 29 October 1923, modelled on the reforms initiated by its founder and first president, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk. Turkey remained neutral during most of World War II, but was involved in the Korean War. Several military interventions interfered with the transition to a multi-party system.

Turkey is an upper-middle-income and emerging country; its economy is the world's 16th-largest by nominal and 11th-largest by PPP-adjusted GDP. As the 15th-largest electricity producer in the world, Turkey aims to become a hub for regional energy transportation. It is a unitary presidential republic. Turkey is a founding member of the OECD, G20, and Organization of Turkic States. With a geopolitically significant location, Turkey is a NATO member and has its second-largest military personnel. It may be recognized as an emerging, a middle, and a regional power. As an EU candidate, Turkey is part of the EU Customs Union.

Turkey has coastal plains, a high central plateau, and various mountain ranges with rising elevation eastwards. Turkey's climate is diverse, ranging from Mediterranean and other temperate climates to semi-arid and continental types. Home to three biodiversity hotspots, Turkey is prone to frequent earthquakes and is highly vulnerable to climate change.[24][25][26] Turkey has a universal healthcare system, growing access to education, and increasing levels of innovativeness.[27][28][29] It is a leading TV content exporter.[30] With numerous UNESCO World Heritage sites and intangible cultural heritage inscriptions, and a rich and diverse cuisine, Turkey is the fourth most visited country in the world.

Etymology
Main articles: Name of Turkey and Turkic peoples § Etymology

Turchia, meaning "the land of the Turks", had begun to be used in European texts for Anatolia by the end of the 12th century.[31][32][33] As a word in Turkic languages, Turk may mean "strong, strength, ripe" or "flourishing, in full strength".[34] It may also mean ripe as in for a fruit or "in the prime of life, young, and vigorous" for a person.[35] As an ethnonym, the etymology is still unknown.[36] In addition to usage in languages such as Chinese in the 6th century,[33] the earliest mention of Turk (𐱅𐰇𐰺𐰜, türü̲k̲; or 𐱅𐰇𐰼𐰚, türk/tẄrk) in Turkic languages comes from the Second Turkic Khaganate.[37]

In Byzantine sources in the 10th century, the name Tourkia was used for defining two medieval states: Hungary (Western Tourkia); and Khazaria (Eastern Tourkia).[38][39] The Mamluk Sultanate, with its ruling elite of Turkic origin, was called the "State of the Turks" (Dawlat at-Turk, or Dawlat al-Atrāk, or Dawlat-at-Turkiyya).[40] Turkestan, also meaning the "land of the Turks", was used for a historic region in Central Asia.[41]

Middle English usage of Turkye or Turkeye is found in The Book of the Duchess (written in 1369–1372) to refer to Anatolia or the Ottoman Empire.[42] The modern spelling Turkey dates back to at least 1719.[43] The bird called turkey was named as such due to trade of guineafowl from Turkey to England.[33] By the mid-19th century, the name Turkey was sometimes used in referring to international treaties of the Ottoman Empire.[44] In 1920, the Government of the Grand National Assembly adopted the name Türkiye Devleti ("State of Turkey").[45] With the Treaty of Alexandropol of December 1920, the name Türkiye entered international documents for the first time. In the treaty signed with Afghanistan in 1921, the expression Devlet-i Âliyye-i Türkiyye ("Sublime Turkish State") was used, likened to the Ottoman Empire's name.[46]

Upon the proclamation of the republic on 29 October 1923, the name Türkiye Cumhuriyeti (توركيه جمهوريتى) was adopted. In December 2021, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan called for expanded official usage of Türkiye, saying that Türkiye "represents and expresses the culture, civilization, and values of the Turkish nation in the best way".[47] In May 2022, the Turkish government requested the United Nations and other international organizations to use Republic of Türkiye officially in English; the UN agreed.[48][49][50] Until 2022, its official English name remained the Republic of Turkey. Though not official, the term Turkish Republic is sometimes used in descriptive, historic, or academic contexts.

History
Main article: History of Turkey
See also: History of Anatolia, History of Thrace, and Ancient regions of Anatolia
Some henges at Göbekli Tepe were erected as far back as 9600 BC, predating those of Stonehenge by over seven millennia.[51]
Prehistory and ancient history
Main articles: Prehistory of Anatolia and Prehistory of Southeast Europe
See also: Hattians, Hittites, Luwians, and Pala (Anatolia)
Map of the Hittite Empire at its greatest extent, with Hittite rule c. 1300 BC

Present-day Turkey has been inhabited by modern humans since the late Paleolithic period and contains some of the world's oldest Neolithic sites.[11][52] Göbekli Tepe is close to 12,000 years old.[11] Parts of Anatolia include the Fertile Crescent, an origin of agriculture.[53] Other important Anatolian Neolithic sites include Çatalhöyük and Alaca Höyük.[54] Neolithic Anatolian farmers differed genetically from farmers in Iran and Jordan Valley.[55] These early Anatolian farmers also migrated into Europe, starting around 9,000 years ago.[55][56][57] Troy's earliest layers go back to around 4500 BC.[54]

Anatolia's historical records start with clay tablets from approximately around 2000 BC that were found in modern-day Kültepe.[58] These tablets belonged to an Assyrian trade colony.[58] The languages in Anatolia at that time included Hattian, Hurrian, Hittite, Luwian, and Palaic.[59] Hattian was a language indigenous to Anatolia, with no known modern-day connections.[59][60] Hurrian language was used in northern Syria.[59] Hittite, Palaic, and Luwian languages were "the oldest written Indo-European languages",[61] forming the Anatolian sub-group.[62][c]

Hattian rulers were gradually replaced by Hittite rulers.[58] The Hittite kingdom was a large kingdom in Central Anatolia, with its capital of Hattusa.[58] It co-existed in Anatolia with Palaians and Luwians, approximately between 1700 and 1200 BC.[58] As the Hittite kingdom was disintegrating, further waves of Indo-European peoples migrated from southeastern Europe, which was followed by warfare.[66] The Thracians were also present in modern-day Turkish Thrace.[67] It is not known if the Trojan War is based on historical events.[68] Troy's Late Bronze Age layers matches most with Iliad's story.[69]

Early classical antiquity
Main article: Classical Anatolia
See also: Phrygia, Lydia, Lycia, Caria, Urartu, Achaemenid Empire, Hellenization, and Hellenistic period
The Lycian Way is a 760 kilometers (470 mi) long hiking path in Southwestern Turkey.[70]

Around 750 BC, Phrygia had been established, with its two centers in Gordium and modern-day Kayseri.[71] Phrygians spoke an Indo-European language, which was closer to Greek than Anatolian languages.[62] Phrygians shared Anatolia with Neo-Hittites and Urartu. Luwian-speakers were probably the majority in various Anatolian Neo-Hittite states.[72] Urartians spoke a non-Indo-European language and their capital was around Lake Van.[73][71] Urartu and Phrygia fell in seventh century BC.[71][74] They were replaced by Carians, Lycians and Lydians.[74] These three cultures "can be considered a reassertion of the ancient, indigenous culture of the Hattian cities of Anatolia".[74]

In the late Bronze Age, there were three[75] or four[76] Greek-speaking settlements in Anatolia, including Miletus.[75][76] Around 1000 BC, Greeks started migrating to the west coast of Anatolia.[71] These eastern Greek settlements played a vital role in shaping the Archaic Greek civilization;[71][77] important cities included Miletus, Ephesus, Halicarnassus, Smyrna (now İzmir) and Byzantium (now Istanbul).[78] These settlements were grouped as Aeolis, Ionia, and Doris, after the specific Greek groups that settled them.[79][80] Further Greek colonization in Anatolia was led by Miletus and Megara in 750–480 BC.[81]

The Library of Celsus in Ephesus was built by the Romans in 114–117.[82]

Cyrus attacked eastern Anatolia in 547 BC, and Achaemenid Empire eventually expanded into western Anatolia.[74] In the east, the Armenian province was part of the Achaemenid Empire.[71] Following the Greco-Persian Wars, the Greek city-states of the Anatolian Aegean coast regained independence, but most of the interior stayed part of the Achaemenid Empire.[74] Two of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, the Temple of Artemis in Ephesus, and the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, were located in Anatolia.[83]

Following the victories of Alexander in 334 BC and 333 BC, the Achaemenid Empire collapsed.[74] This led to increasing cultural homogeneity and Hellenization of Anatolia,[84][85][86] which met resistance in some places.[87] Following Alexander's death, the Seleucids ruled large parts of Anatolia, while native Anatolian states emerged in the Marmara and Black Sea areas. In eastern Anatolia, the kingdom of Armenia appeared.[88] In third century BC, Celts invaded central Anatolia and continued as a major ethnic group in the area for around 200 years. They were known as the Galatians.[89]

Rome and Byzantine Empire
Main articles: Classical Anatolia and Byzantine Anatolia
See also: Roman Republic, Roman Empire, Romanization of Anatolia, Christianity in Turkey, and Byzantine Empire
The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire in 555 under Justinian the Great, at its greatest extent

When Pergamon requested assistance in its conflict with the Seleucids, Rome intervened in Anatolia in the second century BC. Without an heir, Pergamum's king left the kingdom to Rome, which was annexed as province of Asia. Roman influence grew in Anatolia afterwards.[90] Following Asiatic Vespers massacre, and Mithridatic Wars with Pontus, Rome emerged victorious. Around the 1st century BC, Rome expanded into parts of Pontus and Bithynia, while turning rest of Anatolian states into Roman satellites.[91] Several conflicts with Parthians ensued, with peace and wars alternating.[92]

According to Acts of the Apostles, early Christian Church had significant growth in Anatolia because of St Paul's efforts. Letters from St. Paul in Anatolia comprise the oldest Christian literature.[93] Under Roman authority, ecumenical councils such as Council of Nicaea (Iznik) in 325 served as a guide for developing "orthodox expressions of basic Christian teachings".[93]

The Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (now Istanbul) was built by the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian the Great in 532–537.[94]

The Byzantine Empire, also referred to as the Eastern Roman Empire, was the continuation of the Roman Empire centered in Constantinople during Late Antiquity and the Middle Ages. The eastern half of the Empire survived the conditions that caused the fall of the West in the 5th century AD, and continued to exist until the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Empire in 1453. During most of its existence, the empire remained the most powerful economic, cultural, and military force in the Mediterranean world. The term Byzantine Empire was only coined following the empire's demise; its citizens referred to the polity as the "Roman Empire" and to themselves as Romans. Due to the imperial seat's move from Rome to Byzantium, the adoption of Christianity as the state religion, and the predominance of Greek instead of Latin, modern historians continue to make a distinction between the earlier Roman Empire and the later Byzantine Empire.[citation needed]

In the early Byzantine Empire period, the Anatolian coastal areas were Greek speaking. In addition to natives, interior Anatolia had diverse groups such as Goths, Celts, Persians and Jews. Interior Anatolia had been "heavily Hellenized".[95] Anatolian languages eventually became extinct after Hellenization of Anatolia.[96]

Seljuks and Anatolian beyliks
Main articles: Seljuk Empire, Sultanate of Rum, and Anatolian beyliks
Further information: Turkic migration, Oghuz Turks, and Turkification

According to historians and linguists, the Proto-Turkic language originated in Central-East Asia.[97] Initially, Proto-Turkic speakers were potentially both hunter-gatherers and farmers; they later became nomadic pastoralists.[97] Early and medieval Turkic groups exhibited a wide range of both East Asian and West Eurasian physical appearances and genetic origins, in part through long-term contact with neighboring peoples such as Iranic, Mongolic, Tocharian, Uralic, and Yeniseian peoples.[98] During the 9th and 10th centuries CE, the Oghuz were a Turkic group that lived in the Caspian and Aral steppes.[99] Partly due to pressure from the Kipchaks, the Oghuz migrated into Iran and Transoxiana.[99] They mixed with Iranic-speaking groups in the area and converted to Islam.[99] Oghuz Turks were also known as Turkmen or Turkoman.[100][99]

A map of independent Turkish principalities in Anatolia during the 14th century

The ruling family of the Seljuks originated from the Kınık branch of the Oghuz Turks.[101] In 1040, the Seljuks defeated the Ghaznavids at the Battle of Dandanaqan and established the Seljuk Empire in Greater Khorasan.[102] Baghdad, the Abbasid Caliphate's capital and center of the Islamic world, was taken by Seljuks in 1055.[100] Given the role Khurasani traditions played in art, culture, and political traditions in the empire, the Seljuk period is described as a mixture of "Turkish, Persian and Islamic influences".[103] In the latter half of the 11th century, the Seljuk Turks began penetrating into medieval Armenia and Anatolia.[100] At the time, Anatolia was a diverse and largely Greek-speaking region after previously being Hellenized.[104][105][95]

The Seljuk Turks defeated the Byzantines at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, and later established the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum.[106] During this period, there were also Turkish principalities such as Danishmendids.[107] Seljuk arrival started the Turkification process in Anatolia;[105][67] there were Turkic/Turkish migrations, intermarriages, and conversions into Islam.[108][109] The shift took several centuries and happened gradually.[110][111] Members of Islamic mysticism orders, such as Mevlevi Order, played a role in the Islamization of the diverse people of Anatolia.[112][113] Seljuk expansion was one of the reasons for the Crusades.[114] In 13th century, there was a second significant wave of Turkic migration, as people fled Mongol expansion.[115][116] Seljuk sultanate was defeated by the Mongols at the Battle of Köse Dağ in 1243 and disappeared by the beginning of the 14th century. It was replaced by various Turkish principalities.[16][117]

Ottoman Empire
Main article: Ottoman Empire
The Ottoman Empire at its greatest European extent, in 1683, during the Battle of Vienna

Based around Söğüt, Ottoman Beylik was founded by Osman I in the early 14th century.[118] According to Ottoman chroniclers, Osman descended from the Kayı tribe of the Oghuz Turks.[119] Ottomans started annexing the nearby Turkish beyliks (principalities) in Anatolia and expanded into the Balkans.[120] Mehmed II completed Ottoman conquest of the Byzantine Empire by capturing its capital, Constantinople, on 29 May 1453.[121] Selim I united Anatolia under Ottoman rule.[122] Turkification continued as Ottomans mixed with various indigenous people in Anatolia and the Balkans.[119]

The Ottoman Empire was a global power during the reigns of Selim I and Suleiman the Magnificent.[122][123] In the 16th and 17th centuries, Sephardic Jews moved into Ottoman Empire following their expulsion from Spain.[124] From the second half of the 18th century onwards, the Ottoman Empire began to decline. The Tanzimat reforms, initiated by Mahmud II in 1839, aimed to modernize the Ottoman state in line with the progress that had been made in Western Europe. The Ottoman constitution of 1876 was the first among Muslim states, but was short-lived.[125][126]

Topkapı Palace and Dolmabahçe Palace were the primary residences of the Ottoman sultans in Istanbul between 1465 and 1856[127] and 1856 to 1922,[128] respectively.

As the empire gradually shrank in size, military power and wealth; especially after the Ottoman economic crisis and default in 1875[129] which led to uprisings in the Balkan provinces that culminated in the Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878). The decline of the Ottoman Empire led to a rise in nationalist sentiment among its various subject peoples, leading to increased ethnic tensions which occasionally burst into violence, such as the Hamidian massacres of Armenians, which claimed up to 300,000 lives.[130][better source needed] Ottoman territories in Europe (Rumelia) were lost in the First Balkan War (1912–1913).[131] Ottomans managed to recover some territory in Europe, such as Edirne, in the Second Balkan War (1913).

In the 19th and early 20th centuries, persecution of Muslims during the Ottoman contraction and in the Russian Empire resulted in estimated 5 million deaths,[132][133] with the casualties including Turks.[133] Five to seven or seven to nine million refugees migrated into modern-day Turkey from the Balkans, Caucasus, Crimea, and Mediterranean islands,[134] shifting the center of the Ottoman Empire to Anatolia.[135] In addition to a small number of Jews, the refugees were overwhelmingly Muslim; they were both Turkish and non-Turkish people, such as Circassians and Crimean Tatars.[136][137] Paul Mojzes has called the Balkan Wars an "unrecognized genocide", where multiple sides were both victims and perpetrators.[138] Circassian refugees included the survivors of the Circassian genocide.[139]

Following the 1913 coup d'état, the Three Pashas took control of the Ottoman government. The Ottoman Empire entered World War I on the side of the Central Powers and was ultimately defeated.[140] During the war, the empire's Armenian subjects were deported to Syria as part of the Armenian genocide. As a result, an estimated 600,000[141] to more than 1 million,[141] or up to 1.5 million[142][143][144] Armenians were killed. The Turkish government has refused to acknowledge[20][145] the events as genocide and states that Armenians were only "relocated" from the eastern war zone.[146] Genocidal campaigns were also committed against the empire's other minority groups such as the Assyrians and Greeks.[147][148][149] Following the Armistice of Mudros in 1918, the victorious Allied Powers sought the partition of the Ottoman Empire through the 1920 Treaty of Sèvres.[150]

Turkish Republic
Main article: History of the Republic of Turkey
Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and the first president of the Turkish Republic

The occupation of Istanbul (1918) and İzmir (1919) by the Allies in the aftermath of World War I initiated the Turkish National Movement. Under the leadership of Mustafa Kemal Pasha, a military commander who had distinguished himself during the Battle of Gallipoli, the Turkish War of Independence (1919–1923) was waged with the aim of revoking the terms of the Treaty of Sèvres (1920).[151]

The Turkish Provisional Government in Ankara, which had declared itself the legitimate government of the country on 23 April 1920, started to formalize the legal transition from the old Ottoman into the new Republican political system. The Ankara Government engaged in armed and diplomatic struggle. In 1921–1923, the Armenian, Greek, French, and British armies had been expelled.[152][153][154][155] The military advance and diplomatic success of the Ankara Government resulted in the signing of the Armistice of Mudanya on 11 October 1922. On 1 November 1922, the Turkish Parliament in Ankara formally abolished the Sultanate, thus ending 623 years of monarchical Ottoman rule.

The Treaty of Lausanne of 24 July 1923, which superseded the Treaty of Sèvres,[150][151] led to the international recognition of the sovereignty of the Turkish state as the successor state of the Ottoman Empire. On 4 October 1923, the Allied occupation of Turkey ended with the withdrawal of the last Allied troops from Istanbul. The Turkish Republic was officially proclaimed on 29 October 1923 in Ankara, the country's new capital.[156] The Lausanne Convention stipulated a population exchange between Greece and Turkey.[157]

Mustafa Kemal became the republic's first president and introduced many reforms. The reforms aimed to transform the old religion-based and multi-communal Ottoman monarchy into a Turkish nation state that would be governed as a parliamentary republic under a secular constitution.[158] Women gained the right to vote nationally in 1934.[159] With the Surname Law, the Turkish Parliament bestowed upon Kemal the honorific surname "Atatürk" (Father Turk).[151] Atatürk's reforms caused discontent in some Kurdish and Zaza tribes leading to the Sheikh Said rebellion in 1925[160] and the Dersim rebellion in 1937.[161]

İsmet İnönü became the country's second president following Atatürk's death in 1938. In 1939, the Republic of Hatay voted in favor of joining Turkey with a referendum. Turkey remained neutral during almost all of World War II,[162] but entered the war on the side of the Allies on 23 February 1945.[163] Later that year, Turkey became a charter member of the United Nations.[164] In 1950 Turkey became a member of the Council of Europe. After fighting as part of the UN forces in the Korean War, Turkey joined NATO in 1952, becoming a bulwark against Soviet expansion into the Mediterranean.

Tansu Çiller, Turkey's first female prime minister, attends a European Commission meeting in January 1994.

Military coups or memorandums, which happened in 1960, 1971, 1980, and 1997, complicated Turkey's transition to a democratic multiparty system.[165][166] Between 1960 and the end of the 20th century, the prominent leaders in Turkish politics who achieved multiple election victories were Süleyman Demirel, Bülent Ecevit and Turgut Özal.[citation needed] PKK started a "campaign of terrorist attacks on civilian and military targets" in the 1980s.[167] It is designated as a terrorist organization by Turkey,[168] the United States,[169] and the European Union.[170] Tansu Çiller became the first female prime minister of Turkey in 1993. Turkey applied for full membership of the EEC in 1987, joined the European Union Customs Union in 1995 and started accession negotiations with the European Union in 2005.[171][172] Customs Union had an important impact on the Turkish manufacturing sector.[173][174]

Since 2002, Turkey has been governed by successive governments led by Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's Justice and Development Party (AKP). The party has faced criticism over issues such as increasing centralization of political authority.[175] One of the most prominent examples of these criticisms was the Gezi Park protests in 2013. The demonstrations emerged in response to plans to demolish Istanbul's Gezi Park and construct a shopping mall on the site, as well as broader environmental concerns, but subsequently expanded to include protests over what demonstrators described as democratic backsliding and increasing government control.[176][177] More than a dozen people were killed, many as a result of police brutality.[178]

In 2014, prime minister Recep Tayyip Erdoğan won Turkey's first direct presidential election.[179] On 15 July 2016, an unsuccessful coup attempt tried to oust the government.[180] According to the Turkish government, there are 13,251 arrested or convicted people in jail as of 2024, related to the 2016 coup attempt.[181][182] With a referendum in 2017, the parliamentary republic was replaced by an executive presidential system. The office of the prime minister was abolished, and its powers and duties were transferred to the president. On the referendum day, while the voting was still underway, the Supreme Electoral Council lifted a rule that required each ballot to have an official stamp.[183] The opposition parties claimed that as many as 2.5 million ballots without a stamp were accepted as valid.[183] In 2025 the PKK declared a ceasefire.[184]

In March 2025, the detention and arrest of Istanbul mayor and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem İmamoğlu, along with around 100 other people, was described by the Associated Press as a "dramatic escalation in a crackdown on the opposition and dissenting voices in Turkey."[185] These measures sparked nationwide protests, the largest in Turkey since the 2013 Gezi Park demonstrations, during which 1,879 people were detained.[186] Later, in May 2026 ,the Ankara appeals court declared the CHP primaries' results as void. The court decision removed CHP chairman Özgür Özel and reinstated former leader Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu on an interim basis, a ruling criticized by Human Rights Watch as a major blow to "rule of law, democracy, and human rights".[187]

Geography
Main article: Geography of Turkey
See also: List of national parks of Turkey
Topographic map of Turkey

Turkey covers an area of 783,562 square kilometres (302,535 square miles).[188] With Turkish straits and Sea of Marmara in between, Turkey bridges Western Asia and Southeastern Europe.[189] Turkey's Asian side covers 97% of its surface, and is often called Anatolia.[190] Another definition of Anatolia's eastern boundary is an imprecise line from the Black Sea to Gulf of Iskenderun.[191] Eastern Thrace, Turkey's European side, includes around 15% of the population and covers 3% of the surface area.[192] The country is encircled by seas on three sides: the Aegean Sea to the west, the Black Sea to the north and the Mediterranean Sea to the south.[193] Turkey is bordered by Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Iran to the east.[193] To the south, it's bordered by Syria and Iraq.[194] To the north, its Thracian area is bordered by Greece and Bulgaria.[193]

Turkey is divided into "seven major regions": Marmara, Aegean, Central Anatolia, Black Sea, Eastern Anatolia, Southeastern Anatolia and the Mediterranean.[193] As a general trend, the inland Anatolian Plateau becomes increasingly rugged as it progresses eastward.[195] Mountain ranges include Köroğlu and Pontic mountain ranges to the north, and the Taurus Mountains to the south. The Lakes Region contains some of the largest lakes in Turkey such as Lake Beyşehir and Lake Eğirdir.

Tectonic map of Turkey.[196] Straight lines and lines with triangles denote different types of faults, such as North Anatolian Fault and East Anatolian Fault.

Geographers have used the eastern Anatolian plateau, Iranian plateau, and Armenian plateau terms to refer to the mountainous area around where Arabian and Eurasian tectonic plates merge. The eastern Anatolian plateau and Armenian plateau definitions largely overlap.[197] The Eastern Anatolia region contains Mount Ararat, Turkey's highest point at 5,137 metres (16,854 feet),[198] and Lake Van, the largest lake in the country.[199] Eastern Turkey is home to the sources of rivers such as the Euphrates, Tigris and Aras. The Southeastern Anatolia Region includes the northern plains of Upper Mesopotamia.

Earthquakes happen frequently in Turkey.[25] Almost the entire population lives in areas with varying seismic risk levels, with around 70% in highest or second-highest seismic areas.[200][201] Anatolian plate is bordered by North Anatolian Fault zone to the north; East Anatolian Fault zone and Bitlis–Zagros collision zone to the east; Hellenic and Cyprus subduction zones to the south; and Aegean extensional zone to the west.[202] After 1999 İzmit and 1999 Düzce earthquakes, North Anatolian Fault zone activity "is considered to be one of the most dangerous natural hazards in Turkey".[203] 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquakes were the deadliest in contemporary Turkish history.[204] Turkey is sometimes unfavorably compared to Chile, a country with a similar developmental level that is more successful with earthquake preparedness.[205][206][207]

Biodiversity
Main articles: Wildlife of Turkey, Fauna of Turkey, and Flora and vegetation of Turkey
See also: Environmental issues in Turkey
Tulip is a national flower of Turkey. Emirgan Park in Istanbul hosts Tulip Festival each year.

Turkey has rich biodiversity,[208][209][24] and includes three biodiversity hotspots[209][24] out of the 36 in the world.[24] These are the Mediterranean, Irano-Anatolian, and Caucasus hotspots.[24] Central or Eastern Anatolian steppe ecosystems contain wild animal and plant species whose genetic variation have important implications for the food industry, agriculture, and medicine. Other ecosystems in Turkey include Mediterranean plant types, temperate deciduous forest, and Alpine tundra.[210] An extensive number of species of plants and animals exist in Turkey.[210] These include around 197 mammal species, 420 bird species, 820 marine and freshwater fish species, 130 reptile species, and 10,150 vascular plant species.[211] Some of these are endangered or critically endangered.[210] A lot of the animal and plant species are endemic.[24]

Landscapes in Turkey face a variety of threats and risks such as desertification, soil erosion, declining groundwater levels, and salinization of soil. 27% of Turkey is protected, which includes conservation areas, forests, national parks, biosphere reserves, natural monuments, and historical sites.[212] There are 50 national parks;[213] most visited in 2022 were Marmaris National Park and Beydağları Coastal National Park.[214] As of 2020, Turkey's forests covered 29% of Turkey's surface area.[215] Turkey's forests include globally largest concentrations of Cedrus libani and Mediterranean cypress trees, while Turkey's wetlands are significant for migratory birds.[210]

Climate
Main article: Climate of Turkey
See also: Climate change in Turkey
Clockwise from top left image: yearly total precipitation, yearly average temperatures, and Köppen climate types in Turkey[216]

Turkey's climate is highly varied due to rising overall elevation eastwards and the mountains that run alongside the coasts.[189] Warm summers, "cool to cold" winters, and year-round wet conditions are found in the northern coasts. Rainless and hot summers, and wet, cool to mild winters describe the western and southern coasts of the country.[217] Inland areas feature more severe winters, sharper temperature swings,[217] and relatively low precipitation.[218]

According to the Köppen climate classification, Turkey has 14 distinct climate zones.[216] The Mediterranean climate is found in the Mediterranean, Aegean, Marmara, and Southeastern Anatolia regions of the country. In the Black Sea area, humid subtropical and oceanic climate types are usually found. Large swaths of Central and Eastern Anatolia are classified into semi-arid or continental climate types.[219][220]

Turkey is highly vulnerable to climate change,[26][221] due to socioeconomic, climatic, and geographic factors.[26] This applies to nine out of ten climate vulnerability dimensions, such as "average annual risk to wellbeing".[26] OECD median is two out of ten.[26] Inclusive and swift growth is needed for decreasing vulnerability.[222] Turkey aims to achieve net zero emissions by 2053.[223][224] Accomplishing climate goals would require large investments, but would benefit the economy due to less illness and death from Turkey's air pollution, and less fuel imports.[225]

Government and politics
Main articles: Politics of Turkey and Constitution of Turkey
The Grand National Assembly,
the legislative chamber in Ankara
The Presidential Complex, residence and workplace of the President of Turkey
The Court of Cassation is Turkey's supreme court for reviewing verdicts given by courts of criminal and civil justice.

Turkey is a presidential republic within a multi-party system.[226] Due to Erdoğan's judicial capture, imprisonment of opposition politicians and dissidents, and repression of protest movements, Turkey is not considered a democracy but rather as a competitive or fully authoritarian system.[227][228] The current constitution was approved by referendum in 1982, which determines the government's structure, lays forth the ideals and standards of the state's conduct, and sets out the state's responsibility to its citizens. Furthermore, the constitution specifies the people's rights and obligations, as well as principles for the delegation and exercise of sovereignty that belongs to the people of Turkey.[229]

In the Turkish unitary system, citizens are subject to three levels of government: national, provincial, and local. The local government's duties are commonly split between municipal governments and districts, in which the executive and legislative officials are elected by a plurality vote of citizens by district. Turkey is subdivided into 81 provinces for administrative purposes. Each province is divided into districts, for a total of 973 districts.

National government
Main article: Government of Turkey

The government, regulated by a system of separation of powers as defined by the constitution of Turkey, comprises three branches:

Legislative: The unicameral Parliament makes laws, debates and adopts the budget bills, declares war, approves treaties, proclaims amnesty and pardon, and has the power of impeachment, by which it can remove incumbent members of the government.[230] The Parliament has 600 voting members, each representing a constituency for a five-year term. Parliamentary seats are distributed among the provinces by population, conforming with the census apportionment.
Executive: The president is the commander-in-chief of the military, can veto legislative bills before they become law (subject to parliamentary override), can issue presidential decrees on matters regarding executive power with the exception of fundamental rights, individual rights and certain political rights (parliamentary laws prevail presidential decrees), and appoints the members of the Cabinet and other officers, who administer and enforce national laws and policies.[231] The president is elected by direct vote and serves a five-year term. The president cannot run for re-elections after two terms of five-years, unless the parliament prematurely renews the presidential elections during the second term of the President. Elections for the Parliament and presidential elections are held on the same day.
Judicial: The Constitutional Court (for constitutional adjudication and review of individual applications concerning human rights), the Court of Cassation (final decision maker in ordinary judiciary), the Council of State (final decision maker in administrative judiciary) and the Court of Jurisdictional Disputes (for resolving the disputes between courts for constitutional jurisdiction) are the four organizations that are described by the Constitution as supreme courts. The Constitutional Court is composed of fifteen judges and are appointed by the president and the parliament.[5] A member is elected for a term of twelve years and cannot be re-elected. The members of the Constitutional Court are obliged to retire when they are over the age of sixty-five.[232]

The three-branch system is known as the presidential system, in contrast to the parliamentary system where the executive is part of the legislative body.

Administrative divisions
Main article: Administrative divisions of Turkey
Further information: Regions of Turkey and NUTS of Turkey

Turkey is a unitary state. Its administrative system includes central and local administration. Central administration consists of the central government in Ankara, and local departments such as 81 provinces and their subdivisions. Local administration authorities consist of metropolitan municipalities, municipalities, neighborhoods or villages, and special provincial administrations. For economic and geographic reasons, Turkey is also categorized into seven regions and 21 sub-regions.[233]
